title: Permuting Two Arrays
directAnswer: You may permute both arrays freely; you need a pairing where every `A[i] + B[i] >= k`. The hardest pair to satisfy is the smallest A paired with the smallest B, so protect the small A values by giving them the largest B values. Sort A ascending and B descending, then check every index: if all `A[i] + B[i] >= k` it's possible ('YES'), otherwise no pairing works ('NO'). O(n log n) from the sorts.

remember.pattern: Greedy opposite-sort pairing: smallest with largest to maximise the minimum pair sum
remember.formula:
sort A ascending
sort B descending
for i in 0..n-1:
    if A[i] + B[i] < k: return "NO"
return "YES"
rules: You may reorder BOTH arrays independently — the only thing that matters is which A pairs with which B.
Pair the smallest A with the largest B (ascending A against descending B). This maximises the smallest pair sum.
If even this optimal pairing has any `A[i] + B[i] < k`, no permutation can satisfy the constraint → 'NO'.
All n pair sums must reach k; a single failing index sinks the whole answer.
Both arrays have the same length n; each A element pairs with exactly one B element.
whenToUse: Pair two equal-length arrays to satisfy a per-pair threshold on every pair
Maximising the MINIMUM of paired sums (or products) by choosing the pairing
A feasibility (yes/no) question about whether some pairing meets all constraints
Opposite sorting is the natural move (rearrangement inequality, min-side)
antiSignals: You may pick a subset, not pair all elements → selection problem, not full pairing
The threshold applies to the SUM of all pairs, not each pair → totals, sort same direction
Only one array can be permuted with the other fixed → constrained assignment
Pairs interact beyond their own sum → matching / flow
remember.takeaway: To make every pair clear a threshold, defend the weakest links: give the smallest A values the biggest B values. Sort oppositely and check the per-index minimum. If the best pairing fails anywhere, every pairing does — that's the rearrangement-inequality argument for maximising the minimum.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realise both arrays are free to permute, and that pairing smallest-with-largest maximises the weakest pair sum — then a single linear feasibility check decides YES/NO.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting both arrays the same direction (smallest with smallest, which minimises the worst pair), or trying to brute-force permutations.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove via exchange/rearrangement: if a small A is paired with a small B while a large A has a large B, swapping the B's never lowers the minimum pair sum — so opposite sorting is optimal for the min-objective.

problemStatement:
You are given two arrays `A` and `B`, each of `n` integers, and an integer `k`.

You may **permute** the elements of both arrays in any order. Determine whether there exists a permutation such that for **every** index `i`, `A[i] + B[i] >= k`.

Return `"YES"` if such a permutation exists, otherwise `"NO"`.
constraints: Both arrays have the same length n
understanding: Because both arrays can be reordered, the problem is purely about how we pair their elements. We want every pair to reach k, so we worry most about the pairs likely to fall short. Protecting the small A values by matching them with the large B values gives each weak A the strongest possible partner. If even that arrangement leaves some pair under k, no arrangement can succeed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I permute both arrays, or just one?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both, independently. So only the pairing of A-elements to B-elements matters, not the original positions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the threshold apply to each pair or to the total?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: To each pair: every index must satisfy A[i] + B[i] >= k. One failing pair makes the answer NO.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the arrays have the same length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, both are length n, and every A element pairs with exactly one B element.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why pair small A with large B?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The smallest A is the hardest to lift over k, so it deserves the largest B. This maximises the minimum pair sum.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Pairing
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show you see the pairing search, then collapse it with the opposite-sort insight.
hints: Since both arrays can be permuted, fixing A and permuting B covers all pairings. Try every permutation of B against A.
For each permutation, check that all A[i] + B[i] >= k. If any permutation passes, the answer is YES.
There are n! permutations and each check is O(n) → useless beyond tiny n. It exists only to motivate the opposite-sort greedy.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Fixing A and permuting B gives n! pairings; verifying each is O(n). The factorial dominates.
approaches.explanation:
Hold `A` fixed and permute `B` — that explores every possible pairing. For each arrangement, check whether all `A[i] + B[i] >= k`; if any arrangement works, output YES.

**Why it's correct.** Permuting one array against a fixed other enumerates all `n!` pairings, so if a feasible pairing exists, this finds it.

**Why it's hopeless.** `n!` permutations — even `n = 12` is half a billion. With `n` up to 1000 it never runs.

**The structure it reveals.** Among all pairings, the one that gives the *largest possible smallest sum* is small-A-with-large-B. If that arrangement can't clear `k` at every index, no arrangement can; if it can, we're done. So we don't need to try all `n!` — just the opposite-sorted one.
approaches.insight: Feasibility hinges entirely on the pairing that maximises the minimum pair sum. That pairing is opposite-sorted (small A with large B), so one arrangement decides the whole question.

pitfalls: n! blow-up — only feasible for n ≤ ~10.
Permuting both arrays (redundant) instead of fixing one and permuting the other.
Forgetting that ALL pairs must satisfy the threshold, not just one.

approaches.name: Greedy — Sort A Ascending, B Descending, Check Every Pair (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'give the smallest A the biggest B, then verify every pair'.
hints: The pair most at risk of falling below k is the smallest A with the smallest B. Don't let that happen — give small A values large B values.
Sort A ascending and B descending, then pair by index: smallest A with largest B, next-smallest with next-largest, and so on.
Scan once: if any A[i] + B[i] < k the answer is NO; if all reach k it's YES. This pairing maximises the minimum pair sum.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two sorts cost O(n log n) and dominate; the single verification pass is O(n) with only a boolean flag → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort `A` ascending and `B` descending, pair them index-by-index, and check that every `A[i] + B[i] >= k`. If they all do, output YES; otherwise NO.

**Why opposite sorting maximises the minimum pair sum — the exchange argument.** Consider any pairing and look at two pairs `(a₁, b₁)` and `(a₂, b₂)` with `a₁ < a₂` but `b₁ < b₂` (the smaller A got the smaller B — a 'same-direction' pairing). Their two sums are `a₁ + b₁` and `a₂ + b₂`, whose minimum is `a₁ + b₁` (the smallest A with the smallest B). Swap the B values to get `(a₁, b₂)` and `(a₂, b₁)`. The new minimum of the two sums is `min(a₁ + b₂, a₂ + b₁)`. Both of these are `≥ a₁ + b₁`: `a₁ + b₂ > a₁ + b₁` since `b₂ > b₁`, and `a₂ + b₁ > a₁ + b₁` since `a₂ > a₁`. So the swap never lowers the minimum pair sum and can only raise it. Repeatedly applying it sorts A and B into opposite orders — proving that opposite sorting yields the largest achievable minimum pair sum.

**Why that settles feasibility.** A feasible permutation exists iff *some* pairing makes the minimum pair sum `≥ k`. Opposite sorting achieves the maximum possible minimum, so if even it falls short at some index, no pairing can succeed (NO); if it clears k everywhere, we have an explicit witness (YES).

**Why a single failing index is decisive.** The constraint is universal — every pair must reach k. The opposite-sorted pairing already gives each index the best partner it can get for the min-objective, so one sub-`k` sum here means that element simply cannot be lifted to k by any reordering.
approaches.insight: This is the rearrangement inequality applied to the MINIMUM (not the sum): to maximise the smallest paired value, sort the two sequences oppositely. The reusable kernel — 'make every pair clear a bar' → defend the weakest A with the strongest B, then one linear check decides feasibility.

pitfalls: Sorting both arrays the same direction (smallest with smallest) — minimises the worst pair, the opposite of what you want.
Returning YES on the first passing pair instead of requiring ALL pairs to pass.
Integer overflow: 10⁹ + 10⁹ exceeds int; sum as long before comparing to k.

commonMistakes: Sorting both arrays in the same direction, pairing small with small.
Checking only some pairs or returning YES on the first success instead of requiring all pairs.
Overflowing int when adding two values near 10⁹.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Same-direction sorting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Pairing smallest A with smallest B minimises the worst pair sum — the opposite of the goal. Sort B descending against A ascending.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
A = sorted(A)
B = sorted(B)   # both ascending → small + small
return "YES" if all(a + b >= k for a, b in zip(A, B)) else "NO"
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
A = sorted(A)
B = sorted(B, reverse=True)
return "YES" if all(a + b >= k for a, b in zip(A, B)) else "NO"

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning YES too early
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The condition is universal — every pair must reach k. Returning YES on the first passing pair ignores later failures.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on the sum
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A[i] and B[i] can each be 10⁹; their int sum overflows. Add as long before comparing to k.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: if (a[i] + b[i] < k) return "NO";  // int + int can overflow
